analysis.one_liner: Orders the Treasury Department to break up banks too big to fail.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Treasury Department, within one year, to break up any bank or financial company whose failure would damage the economy so badly that the government would have to step in with a taxpayer bailout. It would also have cut those companies off from emergency Federal Reserve lending and barred them from using government-insured deposits for speculative trading. It was introduced in September 2018 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it stayed.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would no longer be on the hook to rescue giant banks whose collapse threatens the whole economy. Small and mid-sized banks would also face competitors no longer large enough to guarantee a government rescue.

how_it_helps.text: The Financial Stability Oversight Council would compile a list of 'too big to fail' entities, including any U.S. bank holding companies identified as systemically important by the Financial Stability Board, and Treasury would have to break them up so their failure no longer threatens the economy without a bailout [S3].

Entities on the list could not use Federal Reserve emergency credit facilities, the discount window, or government capital injections — removing the safety net that makes 'too big to fail' possible [S3].

Big banks could not use government-insured deposits to fund speculative derivatives trading or hedging unrelated to their banking business, and could not put insured deposits or the Deposit Insurance Fund at risk [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest U.S. banks — the ones identified as systemically important — would bear the full cost of being broken into smaller pieces and losing access to Fed backstops and insured-deposit-funded speculation. Their shareholders and executives would lose the scale and implied government support that boost their value.

drawbacks.text: Critics argue that size alone is not the only source of risk, and that a forced, one-year Treasury breakup of the biggest banks could be disruptive to credit markets and large corporate borrowers who rely on the full services of money-center banks [S3].

The blanket ban on Federal Reserve credit for listed entities could tie regulators' hands in a genuine panic, since the discount window exists partly to keep even sound banks liquid during a crisis — a tool created after bank runs in the 1930s [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, widely felt problem — the implicit promise that taxpayers will rescue banks too big to fail, which encourages risky behavior and leaves the public holding the risk. Its remedy is blunt: a mandatory one-year breakup ordered by Treasury with little detail on how to do it safely, and a total Fed-lending ban that could backfire in a crisis. The goal is popular; the implementation is aggressive and untested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on September 28, 2018, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest U.S. banks are better off: they kept their size, their access to Federal Reserve backstops, and the implicit expectation of government rescue. The committee leadership that never scheduled action also avoided a fight over an issue with broad public support.

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing Treasury to break up too-big-to-fail banks and ban their use of insured deposits for speculation

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. Jeb Hensarling, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat for the remainder of the Congress until it expired

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic-sponsored bill with one Democratic cosponsor went to a committee controlled by Republicans, who took no action on it during the two-plus months it had before the Congress ended.

industries.industry: Largest U.S. banks (systemically important bank holding companies)
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to shrink below the threshold where their failure triggers a taxpayer rescue, cut them off from Fed emergency lending, and barred them from trading with insured deposits. Their size and implied government backing are worth tens of billions in cheaper funding, which the bill would have removed.

Breaking up megabanks would reduce the competitive disadvantage of facing rivals seen as government-guaranteed, and a less concentrated banking sector generally means more competition for deposits and loans.
